<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:259598}
Let $r(n)=\#\{(h,k): h,k\ge1,\ u(h)+v(k)=n\}$. For $n\ge1$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $r(n)=0$ iff $n+1$ is a Fibonacci number $\ge2$ \textup{(}\cite{kawsumarng}\textup{)};
\item[(b)] $r(n)=1$ iff $n+1=2F$ for a Fibonacci number $F\ge2$;
\item[(c)] $r(n)=2$ iff $n+1$ is a Lucas number $\ge7$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
With \texttt{rep(h,k,n)} expressing $h,k\ge1$ and $n=u(h)+v(k)$, Walnut returns \texttt{TRUE} for
\begin{verbatim}
                                                          
                                                   
\end{verbatim}
where \texttt{one} and \texttt{two} express ``exactly one'' and ``exactly two'' representations in first-order terms (see the command file).
Walnut also confirms (a).
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:333308}
The set of differences of consecutive elements of $S$ is exactly $\{1,2,3\}$.
The set of differences of consecutive elements of $C$ is exactly $\{1,2,3,5\}$.
In particular, both difference sequences consist of Fibonacci numbers, as Kimberling conjectured.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Walnut decides the statements \texttt{a333308\_gaps} and \texttt{a333309\_gaps} in the command file.
Each asserts that every gap lies in the given set and that every element of the set occurs as a gap.
Both return \texttt{TRUE}.
Removing $3$ from the first set gives \texttt{FALSE}.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
Theorem~\ref{thm:333308} is a translate of known results.
By the identity above, the gaps of $C$ are the terms of A260311 (the gaps of A260317) after its first two terms, which are both $1$.
Shallit~\cite{shallit-cicm} proved with \texttt{Walnut} that every gap of A260317 lies in $\{1,2,3,5\}$ (all four occur) (see also his comments in A260317 and A260311, and~\cite{bosma}), and the gap $1$ occurs again later in A260311 (for example as its tenth term); this gives the second statement.
The gaps of $S$ are those of $T$, and two consecutive elements of $T$ differ by $1$ plus the number of elements of A260317 between them.
Bosma, Bruin, Fokkink, Grube, Reuijl and Tromp~\cite[Lemma~1]{bosma} proved that the tenth gap of A260317 is the last one equal to $1$, so no two consecutive integers $\ge14$ both lie in A260317, and consecutive elements $t<t'$ of $T$ with $t\ge13$ differ by $1$ or $2$.
Since $T$ begins $7,9,12,15,17,18$, the gaps $1$, $2$ and $3$ all occur, and $3$ occurs only twice (in $S$: $7\to10$ and $10\to13$); this gives the first statement.
Our \texttt{Walnut} computation is an independent check.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:lucas}
The sets of differences of consecutive elements are:
\[
\begin{array}{lll}
\toprule
\text{set} & \text{OEIS} & \text{gap set}\\
\midrule
P_{00} & \text{A383423} & \{1,3,4,5,7\}\\
P_{11} & \text{A383424} & \{2,3,5,7,8\}\\
P_{01} & \text{A383425} & \{1,2,3,4,5\}\\
P_{10} & \text{A383426} & \{3,7,8,10\}\\
P_{=} & \text{A383427} & \{1,2,3,5,6\}\\
\bottomrule
\end{array}
\]
These are exactly the sets conjectured by Kimberling.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Walnut returns \texttt{TRUE} for \texttt{a383423}, \dots, \texttt{a383427} in the command file.
Removing $7$ from the first gap set gives \texttt{FALSE}.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
$\mathbf w=0\,\mathbf d$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
For each letter $a$ we have $\sigma(a)=1g_a$ and $\mu(a)=g_a1$, with $g_1=0$ and $g_0=1$.
Hence $1\mu(a)=\sigma(a)1$, and by induction $1\mu(u)=\sigma(u)1$ for every finite word $u$.
Passing to the limit, $1\mu(\mathbf d)=\sigma(\mathbf d)=\mathbf d$.
Therefore $\mu(0\mathbf d)=11\mu(\mathbf d)=1\mathbf d$, and $\mu(1\mathbf d)=01\mu(\mathbf d)=0\mathbf d$.
So $\mu^2(0\mathbf d)=0\mathbf d$.
Since $0\mathbf d$ begins with $0$, it is the fixed point of $\mu^2$ beginning with $0$, which is $\mathbf w$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
